speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, first we need to fill out a personal data record. So I need your last name, which is Leighton, and your first name. Sylvia. Do you have any nicknames?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well my husband calls me Curly.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Curly. I can see why.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's been the last ten years, I guess, since I've been going down to get my hair done.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, and what was your maiden name, Sylvia? Wayne. Wayne? Could you spell that for me?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: W-A-Y-N-E.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, what was the date of your birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: July the 5th, 1912.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And the place?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Butte, Montana.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And your current address?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's Route 2, Box 101, Glenwood. I guess you don't need the zip code.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, I know that. It's not like there's 50 of them for this community. Where did you first live in Washington?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Um, I have to stop and think. Burnett.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Burnett. Do you know how to spell that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: B-U-R-N-E-T-T. That's about 30 miles east of Tacoma. Oh. You know where Carbonado is? Up into Rainier National Park. It's on the, I guess that would be the north side. And Burnett was a coal mining town.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, what did you do there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, my father was a miner. And although he didn't work in the Burnett mines, he worked out in the woods. He had what they used to call miner's consumption. He worked in the Butte copper mines. See, he was an immigrant.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, where was he from? Finland.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh. But his parents were born in Sweden. They're really Swedish. My name should be Johnson. And they came to Finland. Well, Finland was under the Swedish rule at that time. And it was quite a cruel rule. And so they had to change their name and they chose the name Wayne. Hmm. And he worked in the copper mines. He came there when he was 17. Didn't know any English. Had three months education in Finland. And that was where he went to work and where my mother and father met and were married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When you first came to Washington, how did you travel to get here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: By train. Yeah, we came from Butte.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What was that like?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, it was... I don't remember much about it. I was, let's see, I think I was five. And my sister was one. And I suppose I had a good time running up and down the aisles, you know. But I've always liked train. I like to travel on trains.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Who all were your companions on that trip? Just your family?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, just my mother and father. I guess my father came ahead of time. I don't remember, but I imagine he came first and then my mother came with my sister and me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you know anything about your grandparents? Their background?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I do not know much about my fathers. Except that they, you know, as I told you, they migrated from Sweden to Finland. And they had a small farm. And my grandmother lived until she was 91, I believe. She had 13 children. And my mother's mother and father came from Finland and settled in Michigan, Hancock, Michigan. And they came from what you would call middle class. They were Finnish. But their home, both their homes, in Finland, it's not quite up in the northern, but it's not the southern part. But part of the time that territory would be in Russia and part of the time in Finland. My grandmother could have been part Russian, I don't know. But her hair was blue-black and she had black eyes. And my grandfather came to Michigan and he was a foreman in the copper mine there. And my mother... You remember that show on TV about the immigrants coming on the ship? Well, that's why my grandmother came with my mother and her sister, Hilda. They're after these flowers again. I guess.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about your mother? Do you know what her maiden name was?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, and I can't spell it. It's Pickering.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Pickering?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh. I think it's P-I-K-K-E-R-I-A-N. But that's close enough.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, do you know when she was born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Gosh, I don't remember. Let's see. We can count back. In 61 she died. She was 72.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She was 72. Do you know where she was born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was in Finland, but...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, there.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My sister has that information. I don't remember the... They had an estate, and I don't remember what it was called. It's terrible not to know, isn't it? But my sister kept all of those records.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you know what kind of jobs your mom had?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She worked as a clerk in... ...department stores. And that's how she came to Butte. She heard that... Butte was not wild in those days. But it was... ...a town where the men outnumbered the women. I think it was three to one or something like that. And she and her friend decided they wanted to come to Butte to seek their adventure. And she worked in one of the leading department stores in Butte at that time. And Butte was, my mother said, an interesting place. They had their musicals and that sort of thing. And she loved to dance. So she came to Butte to work in the department store there. And that's all. Well, then when my father passed away, she worked... ...at Bridges Clinic in Tacoma Cleaning. As she was called the... ...housekeeper. And that's when she and my stepfather were... ...were married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What year was your mother married? Your mom and dad? Do you know that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, let's see. Must have been in 1910.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, what was your father's name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: His name was Charlie... ...G. Wayne.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you know when he was born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, he would be just at seven years to my mother's age. Okay. I think you can... I've heard my mother say that he was seven years old. He was 42 when he passed away.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Would that have been due to his working in the mines all his life?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, he had... You know, they called it miners' consumption, but what it was was emphysema. You know, like... Like people that live... that work in... ...well, it's something like coal. But copper is so very heavy, you know. They would settle in the lungs and... ...fill up the air sacs. And... He could draw in... Let's see. It was difficult for the lung to expand and contract, you know. In other words, the lungs were not elastic as they were before.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He was also born in Finland then? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But he was born in the southern part of Finland, near Helsinki.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. What was the date of his death?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was April... Oh, it was April the first... Let's see. 19... It had to be 27. Was that when Lindbergh flew across the Atlantic? It was somewhere in there. No, wait a minute. Not 1927. Because I graduated from high school in 30. 26... 25, 24... No, it had to be 22. And we were living in Tacoma then.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So he was a copper miner and he didn't ever hold any other jobs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, then when he... Well, he worked out as a logger for a while. And then we... They bought a little 10-acre farm... ...between Buckley and Burnett.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. How about your brothers and sisters?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have one sister. Her name is Anita. And I have a half-brother, Arnie. Helene. H-E-L-I-N.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Okay, your spouse's name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: William R.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: William R. And the date of his birth?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Place? Where was he born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Here in the ranch.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, really? Yep. So this ranch has been in the Leighton family a long time then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. They came here in 1905.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Grandmother Leighton wrote a poem. They moved... They came from Nebraska. And she was born in Michigan. Wayland, Michigan. And Bill's grandfather was born in England. But came to the United States when he was just a boy. And they were married, and Grandma Leighton was the teacher.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh. They were in the family. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And they moved to Nebraska, lived there for a while, she taught there. And then he wanted to come west. He liked horses. He was an excellent judge of good horses. And of course, that's my daughter, falls right into that. And he came here. And he heard about all the, you know, the Snowdon area? That was then called Missouri Flats. So he got a job working in a mill. And they homesteaded there at Missouri Flats. And Bill's grandmother came with Bill's father when James was five. And she came by boat to Lyle. There were no roads, you see. By boat? By boat, yeah. She came by train to Portland and had to come up the river. Or to the Dalles, I've forgotten which it was. Anyway, she speaks of coming into Lyle. And there was only one cabin. And next, her... I think it was her brother. Or her sister and brother-in-law, that's it, Barlow, lived in Lyle. Or near Lyle. And next morning, they helped her go up to Snowdon. And she speaks in her poem about crossing the bridge there at Klickitat and coming up over the hill to the homestead. And it was a log cabin. And the first winter, they had... I think they had, I don't know whether it was ten cows and a heifer. And that was the year of the terrible storm. And they didn't have enough hay and they lost all the cattle. Except for the one heifer, they kept alive by taking the straw out of their beds. Oh, no. And she said that they built that cabin. And they did have a floor. And they had a window. But it was made of logs. And she talked that first spring. And they moved to Portland during the Panic of 18... Was that in 1896? Somewhere there. And Grandfather Leighton had to have a job. So they moved to Portland. And she said they moved 16 times in Portland. Because they had to rent enough for one month and they had to move.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, no.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And they had one rindle cow. That's the way they had their milk. And it was the job of the children to pasture that cow in vacant lots. And that's where they had the milk. Well, then they came back and they moved to... They bought or rented the stump place here in the valley. And they stayed with Krebses. That's why Krebses and Leightons have been such good friends. And then they heard this place was for sale. And there was only this one ranch. You see there are two ranches here. This is what they call the Turner Ranch. And the other is the whole ranch. And they bought this in 1905.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What was the Panic of 1897?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, times were hard. I think it was in 1897 or 96. I've forgotten some of my American history. But times were very hard. And Grandfather Leighton had... Were they oxen or horses? I can't remember. I think they were horses. And that's why he earned his living by moving, hauling things with his horses. He was able to feed the family, but they didn't have much.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, so Bill's always been a farmer or rancher. Rancher. Did he ever hold any other kind of jobs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. Oh, for five years he worked for the Forest Service. No, not for five years. It was during that big fire on the... Oh, up from Stephenson. What's that area called? Yalko?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, anyway, they had a big fire there. And he packed for the firefighters. Then he worked for the Cattle Association for five years. He lived in what is the cabin up... that we use when they round up the cattle. And he would spend the summers up there. Because then they had about twenty... They had about fifteen cattlemen. And he had to ride around and see that the cattle were okay. So that's all he has ever done.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When and where were you married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We were married in Tacoma. No, Balls Bowl. Excuse me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How do you spell that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: P-O-U-L-S-B-O. That's north of Bremerton.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, and when was that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: 1941, June 26th. By golly, we passed our wedding anniversary.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You should get... That was yesterday. Well, happy wedding anniversary.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Thank you.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And your children's name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: All right, Mary Anita. That's together. But the A is capitalized. M-A-R-Y. Capital A-N-I-T-A. Addington. And Claudia Hoffbauer. And James Wayne.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When was Mary Anita born?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: 1942, June 29th.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And where?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Hood River.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And her occupation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She's a housewife.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How about Claudia?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Claudia was born June 29th, 1946.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Isn't that amazing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In Hood River. And Jim was born January 25th, 1955.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And he was born in Hood River too then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, the Dalles. He was born on his grandfather's birthday.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, is Claudia a housewife also then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, she's an assistant purchasing agent at the Yakima Community College.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And how about Jim?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He's in with his father as a part-time partner and has a repair shop.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, now let's get into some personal information. How about your own education?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I graduated from, what do you want, just college?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, you graduated from high school in?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: 1930 at Lincoln High School in Tacoma. And then which college? The University of Puget Sound in 1935.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You graduated in 1935? Yeah. And you studied there to be?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: A teacher.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: A teacher. What kinds of jobs have you held?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Just teaching. Oh, well, I better take that back. I was a maid while I was going to school. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Could you tell me a little bit about your teaching experience?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I taught two years at Vaughan. That's V-A-U-G-H-A-N. For two years. I taught math, physics, I guess history if I remember correctly. And that was at the time of depression. And I wanted to get into home economics because every other engineer was teaching. And so I heard about the job here in Glenwood. They wanted someone to teach home economics besides everything else. You see, we had only two teachers here in Glenwood.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When you came here? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Is that right? We had four teachers in the whole school. Two grade school teachers and two high school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How many students were here then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We had 19 in high school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I was principal and teacher and Mr. Holloway was superintendent and teacher. And I... And it was amazing what those kids did. We put out a paper every week. We put out an annual every year. We had a big smoker, a big carnival. They had football, basketball and baseball. The girls had basketball. We put out two plays every year. What else?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you have time for anything besides school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I had time to run around. Oh, you did?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What year was that you came to Glenwood then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: 1939. Okay. That was the beginning of World War II. In fact, when I was boarding the ferry at Long Branch to go to Olympia, they announced that Germany had invaded Belgium. Is that right? Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What other kinds of skills do you have besides being a teacher?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, a housewife. I like sewing and I do a lot of knitting and crocheting.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have any other hobbies besides your craft type? Music. Music? What kind of music?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I took vocal when I was at Vaughan. And also, I took some violin and I played the piano.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How many years did you teach here in Glenwood?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Twenty-three years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were there any clubs or groups you belonged to?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I belonged to the Delta Kappa Gamma. That's an honorary teacher's organization. By the way, how many years have you taught? Now?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah. Five.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Would you be interested if I put your name in?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: For that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. I sure would. I'd be honored. Because it's international. Okay. Thank you. I belong to the Women's Club, and I teach at the Women's Club. Ladies Aid. Oh, and I helped... This was before I went back into teaching. I helped raise money to remodel the church. So I was active in church at that time. Let's see. Cowbells?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Cowbells? What's that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, you see, the cattlemen, like Bill, belongs to the Washington Cattlemen's Association. Well, cowbells is an auxiliary of the cattlemen.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I belong to the retired teachers. Let's see. What else do I... I guess that's about it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that the retired teachers group here in Glenwood?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it's Klickitat County.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Klickitat County? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What kind of awards or honors have you received?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, um... Well, my husband and I were named Cattlemen of the Year.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, how neat. What year is that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In 66.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that's neat.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then I received the... Oh, the government gives grants to go to be re-educated in math, you know. And I went to Vermont. What's it called?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: National Science Foundation. Okay. Well, that's a hard program to get into.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I had about six offers. See, I had one in Portland. I had one at Ohio State. And Vermont. And Texas. And one in California. But they were all either one year or two years. And Vermont was four years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you went all four years?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not all four years. I went two years. And the other two years were... It was a repetition of what I'd had, you know, like calculus hasn't changed. Although two of the professors there at Vermont were rewriting a textbook of modern calculus. And the second year I went back there, well, the one professor received a grant to go to teach in India. So they postponed it. And the only thing I would have liked to have taken was the functions. But we had some of that in the modern algebra. And so I felt I was too close to retirement. Well, my family, both girls were gone and Fay was at University of Washington and left the two boys here. So I felt I couldn't go back the third and fourth year. You didn't have to take it. You could if you wanted to.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What years were that that you went back there then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Sixty-six and sixty-seven.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That hasn't been a long time. No. Okay. Could you tell me a little bit about how you feel about the Glenwood Valley? The kind of community it is?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, you know, I think it's a wonderful place to raise children. Now, I personally missed city life because I was raised in the city. So as far as country life here, I can take it for a while. Then I like to get out.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you get out very often?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, like I flew to California a couple times to visit relatives there, my niece and nephew. Which Bill won't go, so I go. And I went to New York, flew there for my niece's wedding and that sort of thing. But as long as I can get out once a week to White Salmon, I'm fine. But I do feel that all the silence of country life eventually gets to me. I become nervous because I miss traffic, I miss people. Now, I could never live where Mariel lives. To me, that would be the same as if I were in a dungeon or something like that. Because I want to be where people are. So that part of it. But I like the clean air, the mountain is beautiful, but I hate the snow and ice.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't blame you there.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I do not like the winters. I miss the rain of the western part of Washington. You miss it? I love rain. I love to hear it on the roof. But as far as raising children, you couldn't find any better place. So, I can adapt anywhere.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How would you compare the life of a rural woman as to that of an urban woman?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I do think the urban woman has more advantages because you have access to so many cultural things, which a rural woman is deprived of. Although with the automobile now, you can get to, you're not that far away that you're not able to get to concerts and things. Although it does mean that it takes more money. But as of now, living out in the country, I don't think it's any different than living in the suburbs of a city. I think it's comparable. You still have to travel.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, that's true.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I'm so used to now, we're just 35 miles away from any town, so it's not a hardship. But years ago, I imagine, when you had to go by wagon, that was a different story. You had to, you had to like that kind of life. I don't know whether I would have survived on that. But, I always say that a rancher or a farmer is rich in assets and poor in cash. But you never lack for the essentials of life and most comforts. Now, I can buy anything I want in the store. I buy some fruits out of season. Of course, my children are raised. I don't have a big family. But I can buy anything I want as far as food is concerned. We do not raise it here because my husband says, you raise a calf, give that ground to raising a calf and you can buy all the food you want.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you've never...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I've had little gardens, but not anything big. And I never canned any vegetables. I'm a little leery of it. And I've always been able to buy my canned vegetables. But I did can a lot of fruit because Bill's uncle lived with us for six years until he remarried. And I made lots of jam. And of course, during the war, it was difficult to can because you were curtailed on how much sugar. Now, one... I remember the one particular year. In those days, we used to combine oats because they used to feed oats to cattle. See, they used to raise stairs. In those days, they would keep the stairs for three years and then sell them. Now, we're in a cow-calf operation. And so they would always put in about 100 acres of oats. Well, in order to combine, you'd have... we had 17 men come to help. So for three days, I had 17 men here for dinner and supper. And when I went down to the board to get replacement sugar, they gave me three pounds. I said, that's hardly enough to sweeten their Kool-Aid. And they said they were sorry, but that was all I was entitled to. But I had saved some sugar during the winter because I knew that I had to feed these men. Well, it took four pies at noon, two cakes at supper time. Well, you didn't dare give them just a dish of fruit. You had to feed these men, you know. Each rancher would help the other one. And so I suppose what we did was to... We were in competition. Who could set the better table?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you do all the cooking for all those guys yourself?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Bill's aunt came and helped me. It took two of us.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah. That's a lot of people to feed.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, there's 17. And then for haying, we didn't have a baler then. They put up loose hay and I would have, oh, during the summertime, between seven and eight men. At noon, for noon and supper.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So... Can you remember how you spent time with your parents? What kind of a relationship you had with them?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, yes. We had... Our favorite time was during a meal time, you know. We'd talk about what took place. Of course, in those days, you know, the father and mother did most of the discussing. Children didn't take over. But we would tell what we did in school. Of course, my father, having had only three months of education... To him, education was important. So he would ask what we did in school. We had no TV, no radio. We had no phonograph. So we played cards. We learned to play... ...whist. When we were very young. And... One of the enjoyable things I remember was... ...the companionship of friends and relatives and neighbors. There was a great deal of visiting back and forth. And I can remember... This is true of the Finnish people. That if you visited in three homes during the afternoon... ...you were always served coffee and something to eat. Never just plain coffee or plain tea. It was always... ...maybe freshly baked cake or cookies or Finnish sweetbreads. Then they would visit. And I remember we children would... We'd play ball, we'd play hopscotch. We had our games. And it was enjoyable. We didn't have to have a tube to listen to. But we had a lot of visiting. Oh, and then... Certain times of the year they would have... The Finnish people were a great tend to dance. They loved dancing. And they would have a dance. And at midnight they would have a buffet-type table. And there was every type of food that you could imagine. From hot dishes to salads to cakes and pies and cookies. And then when we children would be tired we'd sleep on the benches. And they'd dance until daylight. And... In one community... There at Buckley they had... They'd put on plays, Finnish plays. And of course the Finnish language was spoken among... And I can remember when I was in the first grade I got a spanking from the teacher. I was where I wasn't supposed to be. And because I was spanked I was very sensitive anyway. I began to cry in Finnish. But I can't speak it anymore. Isn't that a shame? I've just been away from it so long. I can understand it when it's spoken. Although the Finnish girl that came to Goldendale... When she spoke to me I could not understand. Because I think what my parents... My mother and stepfather spoke Finnish. And when they did it had become Americanized. And so that might be. And of course my mother has been gone since 1961. And I haven't had a chance to speak it. It's too bad.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, that is.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But I married an Englishman.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you don't need to speak Finnish anyway. How is decision making made in your mom and dad's marriage?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My father was the head of the family. And so when he passed away my mother was really thrown into a... Well, she just didn't know how she was going to cope. Because he had always made the decisions. And she had to... All of a sudden she was left with two children to earn a living. And cope with problems in the world. To my grandmother's to stay. And then she remarried. Because she thought she could not take care of the problems. But after she remarried... When she and my stepfather were married, well, they were both bosses. But then in the meantime she had worked, you see. But not having worked after she was married, well, it made a difference. You know, women in those days were very dependent upon their husbands.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you think they discussed things? Or did he just make the decisions and she had to go along with it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I think they discussed. I can remember them talking. Oh yes. It wasn't any different then. They had their problems and talked them over and so on. But there were some areas, children were abandoned. You were told to go to your room or go outside and play and then they would talk. I suppose about personal things. But on the whole, very happy. I had a very happy childhood except I was very fond of my father. And I lost him when I was twelve. So that was traumatic. But I think that in those days, and I think in rural areas, you have, there is a better relationship between parents and children than there are in the cities because of the fact that most of your rural women are home. Although I worked, but then my work wasn't twelve months.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's true.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I took three months off and my hours weren't that long. That is, I was in school until five o'clock, day after day. But what I mean is that I didn't have to leave home until eight o'clock. Then I was home by five-thirty because I was only a mile away, you see. And you have to travel a great distance.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Who were your childhood companions? Who did you play with when you were young, like in elementary school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, mostly girls. I had one particular friend and she was Finnish. We were living on the farm then and she lived on the farm a short ways away. Her father had a better farm than we did. We played house. There were some other girls. We played with dolls much longer than girls do now. We played house and we played baseball and hopscotch. We even played with marbles. I think that on the whole, children then had to invent their pastimes more than they do now. Now they sit in front of a TV and we went out and made our pastimes. I can remember taking my dolls and dishes and we'd take some rocks and we'd make a house. This is a bedroom, here's a living room, here's a kitchen. We would mix mud and we'd make cakes and put them out in the sun to dry and frost them. We were really playing house. We had our dolls. I can remember my sister and I using our cats as dolls. We'd dress them in dolls' clothes and put them in the buggies. I don't see children doing that sort of thing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's true.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They're growing up too fast. I told my granddaughter about it. We didn't demand attention from our parents that you've got to come and play with me. Mothers didn't have time. They washed clothes on the board. It took all day to wash and it took all day to iron. They had saddle irons and they had to cook three meals a day. Not from opening cans and boxes. Therefore I couldn't go to my mother and say, you've got to entertain me like children do this day and age. I think I would have been spanked if I had demanded that. We had our own playmates and we had toys. We had Christmas and we had dolls but we took care of them. I can remember having a little sewing machine and having a little waffle iron. I used to make waffles on the stove. Things like that, you know. Now this little sewing machine was a Singer. My mother bought it for a dollar. We didn't have to have the expensive toys that they have now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Hmm. How about when you were a teenager? How did your play time change then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, shall I tell you? I still was making doll clothes at 16. Sure. Well, I was living in Tacoma then. My mother had remarried, you see. She was a head of stepfather. The girl next door and I used to... Well, we were sophomores. We'd take out our scraps of material and dress our dolls. Hmm. But that didn't last all year. Then we were busy. You see, by that time we had graduated from what they call middle school. We called it intermediate school then. And we were in our first year in high school. Well, then I joined the Glee Club. And I was named on the L Book as a writer. And I belonged to the girl reserves and girl scouts. And... Now, and I turned out for some of the sports too. Swimming and tennis. And basketball, I think were the ones. And then we had our own social group. Lived around where I lived. And we'd have our parties. We'd make fudge and candy, you know, and taffy. And we'd celebrate each other's birthdays. But we didn't have liquor. We didn't have drugs. There were drugs in school. We knew that. Oh, yes. Yes. There were the drug pushers. You'd see them outside. They weren't right in the school, but outside across the street. Even in the intermediate school. But as long as we were not curious and didn't go over there, we were not bothered. They knew who to approach. And it's like Jim said when he was in Yakima. He said, he wasn't harassed. One fellow said, oh, you'll smoke marijuana before you leave. Jim said, he didn't argue. He said, well, we'll see. And he said, as long as you were not curious and wanted to be where they were and act like you wanted to try it. Well, they left you alone because they didn't want to be caught, you see. And so he said he had no problems that way, and neither did I. I remember in my English class, one girl, at the beginning of the year, I thought acted kind of peculiar, and she was drunk. And I helped her to the restroom. And the teacher wanted to know if I wanted something to give to her. And I said, no, we'd just better let her alone. And we left her in the restroom. But they were in the minority. And we weren't, somehow or other, we didn't have that peer pressure. That they feel they have now. Which I think if they would be independent. And in those days, we didn't have money to dress like everybody else. You dressed what you had. And, oh, I suppose we copied on hairstyle and that, if I remember correctly. I happened to have wavy hair. And I didn't, well, I didn't have money to buy bobby pins. And I didn't cry the blues because I didn't. You make with what you had. That's true. And that's true in the country as well as in the city. And I think this day and age, young people are too, they're, they want to put on appearance. In other words, be like, keep up with the Joneses, I tell them. Yeah. If Susie does such and such, well, Ann's got to do that. And I say that's a bunch of baloney. Be individual. You're an individual and do act as an individual.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: True. What about dating? Did you date or anything about high school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When we were in high school, we didn't, we didn't date. We were together, boys and girls. As I said, we had our group. Oh, we had our crushes, that's true. But then again, you see, in those days, there you had the pressure. You had the, in other words, if you went off alone, immediately, you were typed as being a little fast, you see. And it was sort of a Victorian type of atmosphere. And there were the girls who were what we call fast, that they went with anybody and everybody and suddenly dropped out of school because they were pregnant. But they were, again, were just a minority. But I remember in our group, I think there were equal amount of girls and boys. I think we had about 25 or 30 in the group that we had parties with. And, oh, I imagine, I think we played post office, but it was innocent type. And it was a healthy type of relationship. We didn't feel that we had to live a lifetime before we were out of high school. And as far as sex and so forth, we were all curious. But I happened to be taking science. My real ambition was really to be a doctor. When I was in high school, I was in the biology class and my biology teacher had had pre-medics, had been a pre-med student. And I idolized her and she talked to me and told me, she said, you can make it, get through college first. Well, unfortunately, the depression came and that's what, but I did start in at UPS with the pre-med course. But then I had to switch over to mathematics because my stepfather was laid off. My mother worked for $35 a month at Bridges Clinic and that had to take care of the family. So I was totally dependent on myself to put myself through school. I worked as a maid in the family and that's how I earned my tuition. I walked to school, had very few clothes, two skirts and six blouses in six years. See, it took me six years to go through. I was supposed to have graduated in 34, but I couldn't take a complete 15 hours every semester because I had to work. So, I wish young people this day and age didn't feel that they had to experience sex and so on before they were ready for it. I think that I, it's, as I say, it's not that big a deal and I think that, I don't believe in talking behind doors. I was very open with my children about it. They lived on the farm, they saw animals mating and so on. It's all been very natural and I believe in keeping it natural. As I told my children, I said it's one of the finest experiences in married life. It has to be natural. And consequently, I don't approve of the way it was handled years ago. But I think there's the pill, this day and age, has made it too convenient. I agree. Even the shows and everything else and it's, to me, that's degrading.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I totally agree.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I think it's a personal thing between a man and a woman and it should be kept that way. And I think there'd be less divorces if it were. But it isn't something that you're going to be experiencing it with every Tom, Dick and Harry. True. And which much of it is being done this day and age. I guess I'm a little old fashioned.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh no, if you're old fashioned then so am I, Zoe. But I agree with what you're saying wholeheartedly. The group that you hung around with in high school, was that a homogeneous group? Were you all Finnish?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we were different backgrounds. Even different economic backgrounds. Is that right? Yeah. And I don't think there was another Finnish child, boy or girl, in that group of ours. There were Germans, there were English, in fact my best friend was English. And there were Irish. But they were, most of them from blue class, working people. I believe one of the boys and one of the girls, a father, owned a store, a grocery store or something. But not well to do. Now my brother went to stadium and he was in with all groups that were from the well to do and lawyers' children. In fact, he came very near marrying a judge's daughter. And the grandmother curbed that. Oh really? Oh yeah, sent the girl to Europe. They were ready to announce their engagement.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Hmm, well that's a shame. What kind of responsibilities did you have at home?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, yes, we had no dishwasher, you know. And I had to help hang up clothes, which I detested. And had to help wash windows. In other words, different household chores. And carry in wood and coal. See, we didn't have oil or electric heat.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So, you had wood heat or coal heat then, or a combination? Combination. Combination.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think they started out with wood heat. Wood heat was what we always had. And then it was later, my folks burned coal.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's warmer, I think.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I think it went further too. If I remember correctly, I think my mother said.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Hmm. So you only had the one brother. Did he have chores that were completely different from yours, being a girl? Or were you treated about the same?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, about the time, he was born when I was in junior high. Oh yeah, that's true. And by the time he was in high school, I was at Butler's working. Yes, he had to carry wood in, but he was spoiled. My mother spoiled him. And my sister was gone too. My sister is three years younger than I am. And so by the time he was in high school, she was gone too. And so therefore, he had the wood or the coal to get in. And he didn't have to do any housework.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Because that was the female role? Yeah. When you were a young adult, what did you expect about your future? What did you sort of see yourself doing for the rest of your life?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, when I graduated from college, I was going to devote my whole life to teaching. And I had decided I wasn't going to get married. You had? Oh yeah, that's right. Like you change, you know. And you meet somebody. And when I was at Vaughan, I met a young fellow and we were going to be married. Well, as I said, the depression was at that time, so we had to wait. And I came to Glenwood, well, you know, they say absence makes the heart go fonder. Well, that's a bunch of baloney. Distance and being away can ruin a relationship. I agree. So then we broke up and I met Bill. And then I began to think about family. I wanted family. But you see, young people seem to think, oh, I'll never do this. I'll never go there. Or I'll never go to school. Well, never is a long time. That's true. And I've eluded the word never from my vocabulary now when I say I'll never do that or I'll never speak to him. Because human nature is not such. You change. So I met Bill the first year I was here. Well, it was in January. And from then on, I got thinking about, I was leading him to the altar. Unbeknownst to him.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, he didn't know it, huh?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. You know, that's the female role.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did you lead him to the altar?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, devious ways. Made it so enticing that he couldn't resist. Poor male. They think they're doing the pursuing, but they're so wrong.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that's true.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. Female, you know, is the... Well, don't they call women catty?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Okay. We earned the name, Jossly.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you expect marriage to be like? I mean, was it like you had expected it to be or was it really different?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. It proved to be different. Of course, when you get married, you have stars in your eyes and you're up on cloud three, which you can't be. It's very long because you have to become realistic. Oh, we had our usual problems. And the problems were always economic. Always? Yeah, always. Because of the fact that we were at a... I was at a disadvantage, you might say. Bill spent his life here on the ranch. His grandfather had passed on. His grandmother was alive. And Bill and his uncle lived with the grandmother at the old house that used to be down here. Well, he had... His uncle and grandfather got him started in cattle. And I think when we got... we were married, he may have had six or seven cows. I don't remember. But then again, I... if I wanted... I wasn't extravagant then. We had plenty to eat. But, oh, I budgeted. Yes. I couldn't go to town and buy clothes whenever I wanted. I did a lot of something. But when my... when Marinita was born, I went to the hospital. I was there ten days. Of course, the doctor bills in those days, I think it cost $50 to have Marinita delivered. It was $75 for Claudia and it was $500 for Jim. Oh my God. See, but I was 42 when Jim was born. And I was 30 when Marinita was born. But then that's how you... see, that's inflation. So, oh, the problems we had were not that I was overspending or he was overspending. It was more that, why don't you ask your uncle for a little bit more, see? It was... it was... if you need money, you get it. But when they sold cattle... well, let me go back. When Jim and I... Bill and I were first married, we lived over where boers were. And it was less than a year. And his grandmother passed away. And Uncle Frank came over there and he said, now I want Bill to go into partnership with me. And he said, would you encourage him? So I said, well, I'll try my best, but he'll have to make up his own mind. So I talked to Bill and I told him what his uncle wanted. And his uncle said, I've got to have somebody keep house for me. And he said, it's logical for you and Bill to come and live with me down at the old house. And... which we did then. And... so when... if a group of steers were sold, the money was divided. Until his uncle got married. Somehow or other, then the check wasn't divided because Uncle Frank's wife was a little more extravagant. She had two children to begin with. And they moved this house here and lived here. And it seemed to me that they were spending more than what we were. So it wasn't really equal. And that's when we had the few problems. But nothing serious. It was just, I said, I want to have more than we have. And Bill would say, oh, he was so... He thought so much of his uncle, he couldn't imagine him... depriving him. But I knew. And... but Bill sort of had his head in the sand. Until his uncle passed away. And in the will, his uncle had willed Bill the 60 acres we had bought. And it was because his uncle didn't get around to get the deeds made out. And the state said, well, you'll have to pay inheritance tax on that. And they said you had to pay $1,000 for those 60 acres. And Bill said... Yeah, I think it was... Maybe it was more than that. Maybe it was 700... 7,000. I've forgotten. Anyway... He had told the state... Okay, no, it was $1,000, that was it. And Bill had paid 7,000 for the 60 acres. And he said, that's fine, I'll pay $1,000. But you pay me the 7,000. Well, in the meantime, I had told him to get a lawyer and they got that all straightened out. But it hit Bill below the belt. Because he had placed so much faith. But there again, you see, in-laws.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But that's the type of arguments we had. But to say that a married couple won't ever have arguments, that's a bunch of baloney. If two people never argue, there's something wrong with their relationship. Because you need...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Maybe they don't speak.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, they're not communicating.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And that's true.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I've always said, marriages need a good battle just as the land needs a good thunderstorm. It clears the air.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's a good philosophy to remember.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I think, too, as long as you don't get to throwing or getting out guns. But using words and battling back and forth, I don't see anything wrong with it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did you meet Bill?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I met Bill... The women's club had a dance. And Marielle Krips, somehow or other... Well, hi, Poki. Yes, you don't need to go in. She had asked if I would help at the dance, which I did. I was teaching here. Well, when... All right, get up here. When the dance started, Bill Leaton came in. And Ollie Krips had Bill in tow. And he brought him over where Marielle and I were selling coffee at the counter. And I thought Bill said... I asked your... my old man. But he says, I asked your old man. That's to Marielle, something or other. To go somewhere or something. And I thought Ollie was Bill's dad. Until that was straightened out for me. Well, anyway, I met him at that dance. And he talked just a little while and then went off. And I thought, gee, I sure impressed him. Well, then he got the flu and the cattlemen put on a big dance here. There used to be a dance hall. I think it's where the restaurant is now. And I went with friends, with the man and the woman who owned the house where Debbie Trevino lives. And we went to the dance. But Bill was not there. And he had the flu for a month. Then we had a little dance up at the schoolhouse. And he came to that. And I had come with another fellow. And Bill asked if he could take me home. And I was kind of impressed with him. So I went home with him. The other fellow wasn't very happy. But anyway, from then on we went together.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you go out on dates?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, we used to. They used to have a lot of dances. You know what is the Logs now? Well, they used to have a dance hall there. It was in a circle. And Bill used to take me down there. He had a friend that he used to come around with. The three of us would go. And then on Sundays I would go down to his mother's. And we'd have Sunday supper there. And he would come down. And one time we went to Portland. I don't think we ever went to a show. Bill's not much too... He was never too interested in movies. I saw my first rodeo here in Glenwood. It was here in Glenwood I saw my first Cowboys. And I thought there was a movie on location. And they were local cattlemen had been up to cow camp. And two of them had come down to the store to get something. They hitched their horses there at the Glenwood market. And I got excited and dashed to school and asked some of the kids. In fact, it was Betty Hetrick I asked. She was one of my students. What movie was here? And they couldn't understand what I was talking about. So I described the men and oh they laughed. They said, well they were the local cattlemen. So they were the first cowboys I'd ever seen.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Because you grew up in a city.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In a city and of course we didn't have cattle in Tacoma. And didn't have rodeos in those days there. And so I saw my first rodeo here in 1940.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How'd you like it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I didn't care much for it. You didn't? No. I do not like horses. I'm afraid of them. I tried riding. See I'd never ridden. And Bill had an old mare. She was so wide. And I got up on her. And when she was going down, I was going up. And when she was coming up, I was going down. And oh I couldn't walk when I got off her. And I said, that was it. And my family all ride. They're all riders.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's what I thought.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And in fact, when the children were growing up in those days, they drove the cattle to Quickadap. They'd start from here. About oh just at daylight. And drive the cattle.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: All the way to Quickadap?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: All the way down to Quickadap. Down that Quickadap grade. Going up, you know, up the hill here. And then when they would gather the cattle, six weeks later, they would bring the cattle. And we have, we own, Muriel and Bill and Ollie, Osmer Kuhnelsen, oh about, it's just a little less than two acres. Up what they call Snyder Hill. There. And it's a pretty little place. There's a, it's all fenced because it's used as a corral. And there's a cute little creek goes right by. Little stream, it's not even a creek. Little stream. And they had an old stove there and they had built a table with a bench on either side of it. And they used to camp there. When they'd bring the cattle up. Well my job was to take the picnic dinner. I always had fried chicken, potato salad, and gelton salad, and cake and pie. And lemonade and coffee and baked beans. And potato chips. And I'd bring a tablecloth and put it on the table. And then they would sit down and eat the noon meal while the cattle were resting and grazing in this enclosure. And they call it mothering the cows. Calves get with the right cows. And then the men would, after they got through eating, they would smoke and talk and take a nap. And then by that time the cattle were ready to go on. And then they would be taken halfway. And we used to leave them there, what they called the old Dunker church. Close to Liberty Mountain. And leave them there late in the evening. And I would come along with the car. And they'd load up the horses and come home. And get up 2.30 the next morning at daylight, go and bring them the rest of the way home here where they would vaccinate the calves, mark the calves, and then take them on up here. Well they don't do that anymore. Now they're all trucked. But that was the job. By the time, oh, Mary Anita and Claudia and Jim, oh they learned to ride when they were four and five years old.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Bill must have helped them with that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. And then of course there was Uncle Frank. Well then, when he married, well his two stepchildren, Sylvia and Phillip, and then they had Fay and Frank. Now Frank was called Calvin then. And I can still see Frank. He had a little pony called, it was a spotted pony called Stormy. And here was Frank. He was never fast. But Frank would trail along with his, on his pony with his stick. Frank was about like my cat, Poky. He'd poke along. But it was a good life. It was hard. Like Mary Anita said, they'd be half asleep when they had to get up, but they were on the horses. And of course I, not, being able to ride, I could not tell. If I had been, had learned to ride a horse, I could have taken part on that. But then somebody had to do the cooking, so I guess that was me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You probably enjoyed that more anyway.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh yeah. I'm not fond of horses. Hmm. Hmm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, could you describe your wedding for me?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. I was going to be married in the chapel at my college. In fact, I had asked the president if he would perform the services, and he very graciously consented. Well, in the meantime, Bill's mother became quite ill, and she was under the doctor's care for a week. So I had to write to Dr. Todd and told him that, the circumstances, and I would not be able to come and be married in the chapel, that we'd be married here somewhere. Well, then my folks wrote and said to come there. So Bill said, okay, that'd be fine. So we did. We went to Tacoma and got our license at the courthouse. And my sister had told my folks to bring us, and she said, there's a Lutheran church here, and they can be married in the minister's home. So she made the arrangements, and we drove to Paulsville, and that's where we were married. All I remember of it is that horrible green carpet. But it was very impromptu. My mother and stepfather and my sister were the witnesses, were the only ones there. And then we left there and came to Portland, spent a couple days.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long had you known Bill then, before you got married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I met him in the winter of 1941, 1940, and we were married June of 1941. So it was over a year, year and a half.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Before you had any of your children, were you working then, or were you...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I substituted for a month and a half, until they... See, the teacher who was to take my place was killed in a car accident. And so then they had to find a replacement, and in order to do that, they were not able to at the time school started, so I substituted for a month. And that was all the work I did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you do at home then? What was like your daily routine like?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, the first year I was married, we had no electricity. We lived over there where boars were. You see, electricity was brought into the valley in the summer of 1941. And although, I guess it was PPL lines went through the valley, but the people here would not consent to be hooked up because of the cost. And so then PUD brought the electricity in here. And of course in the meantime, you know, Bonneville Dam and Cooley Dam were built. And there was Northwestern Dam, so they were able to furnish the power for Glenwood. So power has not been here too long.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I didn't know that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The school, when I first came here, had batteries. That's how they had their lights. I lived in one of the little cabins up there where the tavern is, and they had a... I don't know, they still...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The small little cabins?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, two rooms. And it was furnished. And I paid, was it $5 a month? Oh no. No running water, you know. But I did have lights. But they had a Delco plant.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What's that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, Delco plant is... I think it was powered with diesel. And it produced electricity. You know, you can have your own power by having a diesel generator. That generates power. You know, you can do that by taking a... going up in the mountains with a trailer, you know, and having a, what they call, Delco plant.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you had electricity in your cabin.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. But no water. No. There was a shed there that had the toilets and showers for men and women both.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Separate, or they were the same one? It was the same one.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, they were separate, but in the same building. And I can remember, Audrey Eaton lived next door to me. That's how they came. When they first came, they lived in the cabin next to me. And we'd run out. This was two feet of snow. You know, I had to take showers. Oh, dear. Oh, yes. Was the water hot? Oh, yeah. It was heated. It wasn't cold water. And the toilets were there. That's, you know, it was like an outdoor toilet, I suppose you might say. Well, anyway, where I lived, no bathroom. It was an outdoor toilet. And the water was a pump outside. You had a pump. And I had to heat my water, all my water, on the cook stove. And I had a three-gallon bucket. And I always kept it on the stove. And that's how I had my hot water, you see. Well, the first winter that I lived over there...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was that cook stove wood?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. Uh-huh. Yeah, when I speak of cook stove, that's wood. Let's see. That was the second year. That was after Mary Anita was born. Grandmother Leighton was ill. She had her stroke. And Mary Anita was born in June. And that winter, the temperature dropped to 45 below zero here. And that house cracked and popped like a gun. And I told Bill, I said, I'm going to stay up and keep... We had a wood heater, plus a wood stove, a cook stove. And I said, I'm going to shut up the kitchen. There was a door between the dining room and the kitchen. The kitchen was here, dining room there, and the living room here, and the bedroom here. And I said, I'm going to pull Mary Anita's crib. Because she was bald-headed. And I couldn't get through the doorway without taking her to the park. But I got to the park with her head, so it was facing into the... toward the living room. And I kept that fire going. And I sat behind the stove, and I could see my breath. I even brought in the dog. I thought he would freeze out there. Great big black wooly dog. Hey, you dogs! Get back here! They mind me as well. Oh, that's that lady out there. I guess. Lady! Get back here! What's going on? Well, we're talking. Hi. What have you got? Beer? Would you like a...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, no thanks.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Large six. Anyway... I guess you're talking all the time. You've got the door blocked. Yeah, well, you've got to go around the other way. And the next morning, when I woke up, I could find every crack that had that much ice, and that water bucket was frozen solid.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that right? The one that you kept on the stove?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Of course, you know hot water will freeze quicker than cold water. And I didn't know that. I should have emptied it. But anyway, I had a nice bulge. I washed down the board. And... Let's see. What else? We had kerosene lamps, and it was a job to keep those chimneys clean.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That was your job, I suppose.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. And I found out from Bill's mother that you used newspaper to clean your chimneys. And it will make them shine. And it was my job to fill them every... every day. And during that time, that year that we... when Mary Anita was a baby, I decided I was going to give a pinnacle party. That's the type of entertainment we had when we were first married. Each of the families would put on a party during the wintertime, and we'd either make the prizes or get some kind of prizes, and we'd serve a midnight lunch, and we'd have as many as eight or nine tables.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And so I... this was my first party. So here I had my slips. I learned that at Mrs. Butler's. When you put on a party, you don't... do not use just your memory. You must have your slips. So I had slips all over the house. Well, when Bill and I were married, we bought $50 worth of furniture. What did that include? That included a bed, and a mattress, a brand new mattress, and a brand new spring, a dresser, a dining room table, which I sold for $35 to Kathleen Animas 35 years later. So I... Actually, our furniture cost us $15. A kitchen table with four chairs, a little desk, two rocking chairs. That was it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Sure couldn't buy it for that meal, though.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, you can't. That furnished our house. Well, anyway, I found that I needed some extra chairs. Well, I couldn't go out and buy any folding chairs. So I took Applebox and by hand made cushions for them. And made all our... made all my prizes and wrapped them in paper. I had wrapping paper that is, you know, like birthday paper and so on. And I don't remember what I served, but I know they were sandwiches and salads and cakes and coffee. And we had a marvelous time. Good. Now we don't do that anymore. Why? We're too busy listening to TV. You are? Well, sure. No one gives parties anymore. They don't give... I learned to play pinnacle when I came here. And we had a marvelous time. They used to have pinnacle parties at the Grange. That's how they made the money. Well, you couldn't even get people to come anymore. Or that we've got the cars, you go to town.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you think there was a lot more socializing then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, absolutely. Hmm. Well, I'm safe to say that we had between, oh, more than ten parties a year. But it was during the winter, you know, when all you had to do was to feed the cattle and you didn't have the farming to do. During the summer we didn't have it. Hmm. But marvelous times. We used to love to go over to Marielle's because she had the nice house. It was, there were more cattlemen. There was the Liles and there was the Osmakoonosans and the Krepses and Pattons and so on. And then the cattlemen, Glenwood Cattle Association would put on a dinner. And ever so often up here at the tavern, the woman and the man who ran that, they served meals. And I remember the first time I went to was shortly after I was married. And the place guards were by using the brand. Oh. So it was Mr. Brand or Mrs. Brand. Well, I wasn't acquainted with our brand yet. Uh-oh. And all the Krepses laughed. I was looking for my place and he said, come on now, he says, you've got to learn for once and for all what your brand is. And he showed me what it was. So there it was, Mrs. Quarter Circle K.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So now you know what it is.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Now I know what it was. I soon learned what the brand was.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you find that embarrassing when you didn't know what it was? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because I'd never been around where a cattle ranch was. It was all so new, you see. You know, I think nowadays kids are more, they become more embarrassed. They're more self-conscious than when I was growing. We took all this in stride. When we didn't have a new dress to go to the dance, we weren't embarrassed by it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You still went to the dance.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Sure, you went. Stay home, why stay home?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: A lot of kids now prefer to stay home.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's right, and I think that's fooling. Why cut off your nose to spite your face? Right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Wow, this is really interesting. When you were having your children, you said you went to the hospital and stuff. Did you go to town to see the doctor often before that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh yes, monthly. Oh yes, I had the prenatal care. And of course it was, he was a general practitioner. Hood River and White Salmon do not have specialists, you see. But then he was a good doctor. And later went to Portland and specialized in internal medicine. But I had him for both Marion and Claudia. And then Dr. Hardwick left before Claudia was born, so I had Dr. Lewis. And with Jim I had Dr. Mills. Now he was a specialist. And Dr. Mills still, Jim went to him, oh gosh, I think he was in college. He had a bout of sore throat when he came home. I said, well you better go to the doctor. And Dr. Hinkle was day off, I guess, so he went on to the Dalles. And they scheduled him with Dr. Mills. And Dr. Mills says, I've been following you. He says, I read the Glenwood News whenever I can.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's neat.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Of course he delivered quite a few of the babies here in Glenwood. In fact, I think Marilyn Steinbaum or Marilyn Scott's children, I think she went to him. I know that her sister did. So there are quite a few children that have been delivered by Dr. Mills. So it wasn't any different than it is now. Mary Nita's boy was born in White Salmon. And Dr. Hogbert, just as I had with her. I went to Hood River.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What factors do you think affected the number of children you had? Did you want more or less? Did you sort of get what you wanted?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Of course, I was 30 when Mary Nita was born. Well, the war had something to do before we had any more. Because we didn't know whether Bill would be going off. But each time his card would come up, I'd go and they'd say, no, you're essential to the war effort. Because of the ranch. Yeah, the ranch, and his uncle had to have him there. So he wasn't taken. But nevertheless, we waited. We waited four years. And Claudia was born at the end of the war in 1946. Then, before I went back to teaching, we tried again, but I had the misfortune of having a miscarriage. So then we sort of gave up. Jim was afterthought.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where did you get your knowledge about having children and how to raise them? Was that from your mother?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, my mother. She would... And then I took a lot of science. I had biology. I didn't learn it from other people. I read. I got information from the school, from the library. Although you didn't get as much as you do now. But my mother talked to us.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What about raising your children? Do you think you raised your children more or less like you were raised?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I think I was a little more liberal. Although discipline-wise, I suppose my teaching came in there. I try. You see, when I was working at Butler's, I had to babysit. They had a conflict there. Mrs. Butler didn't believe in spankings. Mr. Butler did. And the boy, they had just the one child. And I saw what it did to that child. It made it difficult for me. I was not to strike him or hit him, and yet he would take advantage of the fact that I couldn't. I remember one time he took his piece of watermelon and opened the door and threw it against the wall in the hall. And I had been told that if I can't handle what I'm to do, that I am to pay for what damage is done. And fortunately the paper was washable. So he helped me clean. And it frightened him, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Voluntarily did he help you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, voluntarily. And yet, the last three years I was there, I had an easier time. His folks had the problems with him. But he and I got along fine. And when I left, he cried. And he was 14.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Gee. That's really amazing.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So, I didn't believe in picking up, taking things off the coffee table and putting them up. Either one of them, either of the three, if they tried to pick things that they weren't, I slapped their hands.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you and Bill then, more or less together, decide on discipline and things like that, and the family?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, we agreed on all that. Oh, except one time, he thought it was kind of cute when Claudia went by with her, in her walker. We used to have the walkers then. They were made of wood. She had a bottle and she went on the coffee table like that. And I was quite perturbed. Oh, he said she was having fun.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you think the role of children has changed nowadays since when you had yours? In other words, do your children treat your grandchildren differently than you treated them?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In some sense. I think that, I think my two grandson and granddaughter, I think they're a little mouthy. When I speak of mouthy, I think they talk too much. You know, silence is golden. They have a tendency to interrupt when, not so much Bill as Bernadine. She needs, well, her father is curbing her when he's trying to visit and she's trying to interrupt. He sends her to the room. So, I think it's about the same. I think it depends on the parents, on the people. Some people, well, when mine were growing up and Mrs. Lofgren, a friend of mine, when she was raising hers, she did not believe in spanking. She told me, I ruined my children by slapping their hands. They were not, they couldn't express themselves. I said, they expressed themselves just fine. In other words, they were not creative. Well, I couldn't see where slapping hands would make them not creative. If they were going to be artistic, they'd be artistic, whether you slapped their hands or not. But that wasn't her philosophy. She thought that you should let a child discover himself. You must not do things to discourage him. Consequently, I saw many times when she had to hold her son in her lap, just literally holding him. To keep him from knocking things over or throwing things around in someone's home. When I took my children, they were to understand that they were to leave things alone. They had their toy with them and they were to play with it. But were not to touch anything in the home that we were visiting. Maybe I'm wrong on that, I don't know. No, I agree. But I have seen children come in my home and I've held my breath. Wondering if my son...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: House is going to be still standing.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, in fact, my sister was very lenient with hers. And when she would come, that was with her second boy and her daughter. She said, well, now we better put this up and we better put that up. But by the time she got through putting things up, I didn't have anything around. So, but that's the difference, I guess. And they all grew up and they're all fine.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did you feel when your children first began to leave home? Did it change your life a lot?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, yes it did. It became, it was an adjustment that I had to make. Just as I had to make when the first one was born. That was like a little stranger coming in the home. And demanding attention, bottles and diapers and what have you. And then suddenly they're gone and the table is empty. There's just father in me. And our occupation is letting the two cats in or letting them out. So, it, yes, I shed many a tear. But you can't hold them back. That's not fair. And I've stopped to think of the, when I left, that I saw my mother and stepfather just a few times, maybe once or twice a year. Now I have a daughter who lives in Zillow, I see once or maybe four or five times a year. And it suddenly strikes home, just.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What they went through. Yes. Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think of, they speak of growing old gracefully. No. It's quite a traumatic experience. It's lonely. And as long as you have your husband or you have your wife, that takes up. But, you know, there's a trend now to think of the older people. And the older people that are being abused. It isn't just all child abuse.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's true.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's parent abuse. And I don't, it doesn't necessarily have to be abuse, physical abuse, but emotional abuse. In other words, how often do you call or write? So you remember on your mother.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I do. We, I probably talk to my mom every, oh, at least once every two weeks, but I usually talk to her at least once a week.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, that's good. Of course, when you marry, well, then there has to be an understanding how much you're going to spend. You can't say, okay, I'm just going to talk to my mother and heck with yours. See, then it becomes a problem of priorities.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you do for recreation now then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I have, I don't have any sports. I do now. I have a great deal. I, um. My hobbies is reading. I read a great deal. I have books in every room. In fact, I have a pile of books by my bed. I'm reading three or four of them at a time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What kind of books?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I read fiction and nonfiction, and I take, oh, how many magazines? Well, I have National Geographic. I have the U.S. News. I get every week, and I get the Reader's Digest, McCall's, Ladies' Home Journal, Better Homes and Gardens, Sunset, Flowers and Gardens, Red Book, The Work Basket, Farmer, Farm Journal, Washington Farmer, The Yankee Magazine. I guess that's it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's quite a few to read.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then, I watch some TV, but special programs. But I'm crocheting or knitting when I'm watching.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right on. That's my attitude.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And, uh, I go with Bill wherever, when he has to go down, I go with him. He goes to sales at the, uh, the Dalles, and I go along, and I take my knitting or my reading along. We like to go. We go over to Hood River Inn very often. We average about once a week. We like to go there to have a nice dinner. I like to travel, but Bill doesn't care for it, so I go with my sister. We are planning to go to Hawaii this winter if everything works out all right. So, she told me to save my shekels, so I said okay. That's it. That keeps me busy. I could do more in the house. What the heck with it. Build the house work when I'm dead and gone. I used to be very particular, and when I was working, I got my work done. Um, I'm sorry to say I'm not that good now. I'm not a slave to my house. Now, my daughter, Claudia, she's an immaculate housekeeper. Beautiful housekeeper. And, as I said, I used to. I used to do my washing on Mondays, the ironing on Tuesdays, the mending on Wednesdays. Thursdays, uh, baking, and Friday I'd clean upstairs, and Saturday downstairs, and Sunday I'd watch two men take naps. Mmm. But I don't do that anymore.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You take naps too, huh?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I take naps now too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You know, when you were talking about living over here, when you first had, um, Claudia?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And you, Mary Anita.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mary Anita. Okay, and you didn't have electricity and stuff. You had to wash all your diapers on the boil, and all that kind of stuff?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, and I boiled, uh, um, in those days, now they don't do that anymore, but I boiled all her diapers, and her bottles had to be boiled on the stove.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: On a wood stove.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: On a wood stove, and I boiled her diapers, because her skin was very tender, um, sensitive, and it was to keep her from getting diaper rash. In fact, with all three of them, I boiled their diapers. Now, I did not have an automatic washer until Jim was two years old. Now, I took off. See, Jim was born the twenty, twenty, uh, fifth of January. My last day of teaching was the eighteenth of January. Um, I, um, I was gone six weeks. I went back the first of March. And I had a girl come and, um, take care of him while I taught. And I washed the bottles, and sterilized them, made his formula, washed his diapers. Now, I did this by hand, see, because I didn't have an automatic washer. And to bring out the conversion, the conventional washer every morning, I didn't have time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Conventional, by that you mean?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You know, the, uh, uh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Ringer washer?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, the ringer washer, that, you know, electric. And, uh, in fact, that's what I had to use. And, uh, so, and I boiled him, and hung him out, and cooked breakfast. I got myself ready and went to school and taught.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You must have been up, gotten up in the middle of the night.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, six o'clock. And then, um, uh, of course, uh, I had to stay at school to make my lesson plans and so on. I'd get home about, about, uh, well, I think then I, I would make it home about five. I had dinner to get. The girl I had couldn't wash dishes because her hands broke out. I paid her $150 a month to sit by the bassinet and read comics. But I was forced to. See, I had, from March until end of school. Well, I knew I couldn't, uh, couldn't keep her beyond that. In fact, I was going to quit. And, uh, Becky Boyce's father came down to talk to me. He was on the board. And he said, will you teach a half a day? And in those days, see, I was 42. Almost, well, 43 then. Well, I guess I could do it. I got along all right. I said, okay, I'll teach a half a day. So they hired a new superintendent. And the new superintendent came down and talked to me. He says, well, if you're going to teach a half a day and have to have a babysitter, can't you do it all day? So I said, okay. I don't know whether I could do it. I would do it now if I knew then what I know now. But anyway, I did. And I, uh, got a woman from Camp Draper. I had to. I got, Jim Reddy gave his bath and did his diapers and did his, um, his, uh, bottles and fed him. Drove up to camp to pick up the woman, bring her down here. And by, and by that time I had dressed, ready to go to school. Then I went to school. Then I came back and, uh, I had permission then to, uh, leave at four o'clock. And I picked her up, took her to camp and brought her back again. So I, I thought, well, I can't do that. That was too expensive and, and plowing snow with my car. So, uh, do you know Venita Dean? Mm-hmm. The sweeter Dean. Well, her mother asked if, uh, she could have the job. And I said yes. The lady I had before was not a good disciplinarian. And Jim was about driving her ragged.
