And, uh, he was turning on faucets in the bathroom and doing just, here, just 18 months old. So I told Venita, uh, that was her mother's name. I said, now, Venita, you've got to make a mind. I said, here's a flyswatter. I said, you use it, but don't use it on his head. Use it on his bottom. And I said, that's the seed of learning. Well, she used it twice. And he just loved her, but he doesn't remember Mrs., uh, I can't even think of her name either now that I got from Kathy. But see, Mrs. Steinbaugh made him mine. And she used it twice. Well, that first summer, when I was home, I was swatting flies and broke that flyswatter, and he broke out in tears. And I can still hear him say, oh, Mrs. Steinbaugh will be mad. You broke the flyswatter. I had to go to town and buy a new flyswatter. And that had an honored place in the kitchen. But she never used it after that. And he idolized her. And she was there until he started school when he was, uh, when he was six and a half. Hmm. So, you know, my philosophy is, you do not say never. You'll never do this, or you can't do this, until you have tried. And you'll be surprised what you can accomplish when you set your mind to it. And when I hear these kids nowadays, oh, I don't want to take this, it's boring. I want to kick them in the pants and tell them, listen, you'll be surprised what you can do. And if there's anybody is bored, you're doing it to yourself. Nobody is boring you. So. Hmm. Oh, by the way, have you have a new superintendent yet?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh, yeah. I'll tell you about him in just a minute. Okay. Um, when did you get electricity then?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: 1941. So you weren't without it for a really long period of time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh, I was over there because we were renting and the people who owned it didn't, they were going to put it in, um, later on. But, again, it was, uh, it was money-wise, you see. I mean, they, we only paid $40 a month for rent there and, uh, they didn't feel that, uh, the amount of, um, rent. The old house and Uncle Frank had electricity.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you have indoor plumbing and stuff?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. No.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You still didn't have that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. Didn't have that. We had the old outdoor. And you can imagine in 25 below zero you...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did you go about training, you know, potty training your little ones there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I, uh, I bought a little potty train, a little potty chair.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Because, I mean, you know, in the middle of the night, a little kid to trek them out through the snow and stuff?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, no. No. I had a little, uh, I bought a little potty chair. Yes, they had those. But, uh, as far as, uh, as the adults, we had to go up to the old outhouse.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When did you get indoor plumbing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, then, you see, there was the war again. And you could not get anything. You could not get any plumbing, uh, uh, materials. In fact, we had thought of, we planned to put in, uh, plumbing. And Uncle Frank talked about it. So, um, it wasn't until 1946...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That you got indoor plumbing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That we got indoor plumbing. And then you couldn't get, we were not able to get a bathtub right away. We had to put in a shower. And then a year later we got the bathtub. So then, um, in 1940... 1949... Uh, we did away with the, uh, we, um, sold the, uh, wood stove in the, uh, kitchen. And bought a combination. Electric with a trash burner. It was all built together. And we felt we had to have the trash burner because it would get so cold in the wintertime.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So, in other words, it was like half electric and half you could...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, um...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't understand.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, the electric stove, the oven and everything was electric. But built to it was an iron, cast iron, um, you've seen these trash burners.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, okay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, it was attached to it. And, um, in the wintertime I, uh, I kept firing there. And I had chickens then and I used to cook oats. Have them in the, uh, a bucket. And have it on that, uh, a trash burner and, uh, I'd take hot oats out to my chickens. But I gave that up when I went back to teaching. And, um, we did away with the chickens then.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Who got the wood for you when you lived over here when you were first married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did Bill? Oh, yeah. Yeah, he got it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did he bring it in the house or did you have to bring it in?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, no, he did it. Now, when we moved back to the old house, when they would finish, uh, feeding the cattle. And then they had a lot of horses. They used horses to haul hay with, you see, and plow and so on until... Oh, gosh. I don't remember whether it was after... it must have been after the war when they got their first, um... Maybe they had a tractor before the war. You know, before America was involved in the war. I don't remember now. But anyway, they had quite a few horses they had to take care of. And then the cow had to be milked. So one milked the cow and the other cut wood. And it was always to cut enough wood for the kitchen stove and for the living room stove. And that was piled there on the porch. It was an L-shaped porch. And they never thought of coming in without... Without doing it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you bring it in from the porch then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: In the kitchen, they had... They built right into the kitchen wall, which faced west, a wood box. Oh. So there was a lid in the kitchen, there was a lid outside, you see, and you opened it up and there was... And it was, oh, about that high. So it held lots of wood. So that's where I got my wood for the...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How convenient.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes, it was. And... But for the living room, you had to go out on the porch and get the wood. So I kept me busy keeping both stoves. Then... In 1947, we bought an oil heater. And we've had oil ever since. But prior to that, the first heater we had in the living room was the one Uncle Frank had. You put wood in from the side. It was kind of ornate. And then we bought what they called a circulating wood stove. You could put wood in and you could keep wood in there, keep fire in there. Most of the night. Hmm. So that, as far as having to ever chop wood, I didn't ever have to. I doubt if I... Well, I couldn't even now. Chop wood. And it's the same thing when they go up to ride at the cow camp. Before they come in to eat or to start supper, see the men cook for themselves up there. And by the way, they have the banker and they have the judge up there. And they have their chores to do, cut wood and cook. And that's their vacation. They love it. But they cut the wood and take care of their horses and then come in and cook their meal. Except on the night, on the first couple nights, I do it for them. I stay up there and cook for them. But then I come home. And after they've eaten, they wash the dishes. They play cards. They have a wonderful time up there. Now I don't know what they're going to do. You can't go up there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Because of the mountain, you mean?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. You have to have... Bill and Jim are going to have to fix fence up there along with Bill Gersh. And they're going to have to have a forest service man go with them with a radio. Otherwise we'd have to buy radios. They're quite expensive.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What kind of radio do they need? Just a CB radio?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no. CB is special. And you can't be any further than 30 minutes from the vehicle. So I don't know what's going to happen.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's going to really affect their schedule.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But anyway, Bill says, well, we'll cross that bridge when we get to it. So that'll be last of September. I hope the mountain goes to sleep. But I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You said that the depression really affected your going to school. Do you think... were there any other effects that it had on you then? Or how about now? Do you think there are any effects? Anything happen to you because of the depression that's changed the way your life has been since?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I think that... Oh, the depression was not a fun thing by any means. I'd hate to see any of you young people... It's like Mary Anita says, that if another depression comes, like the one in the 30s, she says, Mom, I don't know how we'd ever cope with it, and I don't either. But you did what you had to. But it did make me independent. Now, I didn't have to... in fact, I couldn't have borrowed any money. I had a little savings account. I think I must have had, I don't know, $50. And I lost that when the banks closed, you know. And it was... they paid back some of the larger amounts, but not the smaller.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Which was important to you at the time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and that was in Tacoma. You know, I saved... we used to have bank day at high school every Tuesday. You'd bank your nickels and pennies and so on. Well, that's what I did. And I lost every bit of that. I was going to go to Ellensburg to school, and I don't know what $50 would have done, but it would have been start anyway. But butlers told me that I'd be far better off staying there and live with them and go to UPS. And Mr. Butler said he had excellent rating. And he said, I think you'd be far better. And it has. And it did. Because when I would mention I'm a graduate of College of Puget Sound, well, immediately that opened some doors, you see. So I can't say that... other than I was not able to pursue medicine, which probably on the way somewhere or other I would have had to give it up anyway. I would not say that it ruined my life or anything like that. In fact, I think I benefited by it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How do you say... how do you figure that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, because I was self-supporting.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you learned to do for yourself. So like you never really worried when you were married, like if something would happen to Bill, what you'd do, because you had a profession.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I had a profession. I had my degree. And not only that, but I was forced to work in a family where I would never have had the opportunity to hear Paderewski play. I would never have had the opportunity to hear the outstanding violinist, nor to hear the Seattle Symphony Orchestra and the Tacoma. I guess it was the Philmonic Orchestra at that time. I also saw the Russian ballet. See, these were tickets. Mr. Butler being manager of the Kelly Clark...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And this was all during the Depression.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: This is all during the Depression. Mr. Butler was manager of Kelly Clark food brokers. I don't know whether they're still in existence or not there. And as a civic community worker and an important person in Tacoma, it was understood he'd buy these tickets. Well, many times these engagements would come when they had other engagements. They had dinners or Mr. Butler had to be out of town or something. Well, I fell air to those tickets. And Mrs. Butler didn't care too much for the symphony concerts. So I got all of those. Not only that, but when they would have dinner parties, I was able to meet well-to-do, influential people in Tacoma. Now, one of the persons that I met and was very fond of was the daughter of Weyerhaeuser's, Mrs. Pickham. And she was the trustee of the University of Puget Sound, now her daughter-in-law is. And she would come in the kitchen and talk to me and ask me how school was going, what I was taking. And in fact, the last year that I was there at Butler's, before I left, she said, Sylvia, I want you to understand that if you ever need help, you are to come to me. Well, there may have been times I could have, but then you don't, you know, unless it's absolutely desperate. But she said, you're doing fine, keep it up. She was the one who told me about money. I, oh, like all young people, I used to at times feel sorry for myself. You know, that's understandable. I would get to the point where I was probably tired. I had to be up at 5.30 in the morning, cook breakfast before I went to school, and I studied not till 10 o'clock, but it would be, 12 o'clock was early. Many times, 1, 2, and 3 o'clock in the morning, and I'd be dead for sleep, you see. But I used to think, oh, if I could just... I had been born in a family that had money. So one time she sat down and talked. She was a dummy at her table, and she came in, and she said she used to like to come in and talk to me. This one time came up about money, and I told her, I said, oh, it must be wonderful to have all the money you want. So she said, I'm going to sit here and tell you all about it. She said, yes. She said, I was fortunate, I was born with a silver spoon in my mouth. She said, I've never known what it is to be without money, not having anything I want. But she said, you have to remember that there is a tremendous responsibility. She said, you can have money today, and maybe tomorrow you could be bankrupt. And that can happen. You can be up there, and it's very easy to fall down. And she said, with me now, she said, I have the responsibility to make this money work for me, not let the money control me. And which she did. She did many, she was on many committees, and they contributed to charities in Tacoma, and I guess all over the world. But now she says, my husband was born of a poor family. Really? And she said that we met in college, and she said, he's fortunate, he's got a good job. But she said that he has to work for it, and he realizes that the money isn't everything. It's not all that important, but it's nice to have. So, you see, I got a nice philosophy as far as wealth is concerned. So, when I hear somebody talk about what they have, and how much they have, I always think of Mrs. Tickham, who said, never let money rule your life. You must make money work for you, and do what you want it to do, but not control. Because, she said, otherwise it'll destroy you.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And it can, too. It can. Both lack of it, extreme lack of it, and having too much. That's right. If there's such a thing as having too much.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, well, now, with warehousers, they, well, they're multimillionaires, you know. And they, well, like she says, we never, we have all the money that we want, but then, of course, she says, we're not going to be extravagant either. We're not going to throw it all away either. It must do good. It must do some good. And I, at that time, too, I don't know whether you're aware of the the Mattson kidnapping case that took place in Tacoma. The Mattson boy was kidnapped and killed. It was during the Christmas vacation. And the, his father was a doctor in Tacoma, Dr. Mattson. And they lived right at the bottom of, do you know where the Franklin Mansion is? It used to be the Warehouser Mansion. Well, their home was right at the bottom of it. And the Franklins had bought it from the Warehousers. And there had, the Franklins had a maid. It came out later that she was instrumental in planning the kidnapping of the Franklin boy. And somehow or other, somebody forewarned the Franklins they better take the boy to California, and they did. And they fired the maid. Well, the man who was going to do the kidnapping apparently didn't know that the maid had been fired and that the Franklins were gone. And he entered the home. He gained entrance into the home, found that there wasn't anybody there. And he came down the, you know, there's the rock gardens, you know, down that slope. And he came down the path and opened the French doors to the Matson home and grabbed the, he was 11 years old, and grabbed him. He was in his pajamas. And he and the, his two sisters were there with the housekeeper. His parents were at a party. And they found him a week later. He had been, he was dead. And so you see there, like the Franklins having money, and like Mrs. Titcombe told me, when this case was, they were trying to find the kidnapper, or kidnappers. They really did not know how many were involved. That there was one case of what money can do. It can be a detriment, it can be detrimental to the ones who are in the family, in that there's always the danger of being kidnapped, or blackmailed, or something like that. And she said, you see, we have that to contend with, which she said, you may not have to worry about it at all. She was a wonderful person. So I would not have met people like that if it hadn't been for the depression. So you see, there's always some good to all bad.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Wow. You've had such an interesting life and done so many neat things.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, Claire, everybody's life would be interesting if they... Oh, it gets humdrum, I know. Here, last winter when it was snowing that 37 hours, I nearly went wild. But many times I'll sit in there and stop thinking about what had gone in the past. Oh, there's some regrets. I wish I had been a little closer to my folks, but I chose to come here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So... Can you think of anything else that you would really like to talk about?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I miss my teaching. I miss it dreadfully. But I realize I'm at the age I can't do it. I don't have the energy. And... I think we're living in the most wonderful age. I'm glad I'm living at this time. It was like... One of the retired teachers, we had a luncheon of... Well, every May we have a luncheon at Flying L. That is Delta Kappa Gamma. And this is the May. It's on Saturday. Flora, Mariel, and I have that luncheon. And... We... Elsa fixes the main meal and the salad and the rolls. And we fix the dessert. And we take it out. In the last couple of years, what we have done is to have either ice cream or we've had sherbet this year. We had two kinds of sherbet and we made all kinds of cookies. And we took our tier trays and had them all stacked with cookies. And Mariel fixes the flowers. Now this year she... She used her pink goblets of her Franciscan pottery. I hadn't thought of that. I have those glasses too. And she puts... Oh, she goes out to the meadows and picks the blue camas and other wildflowers plus some of the tame flowers she has in her yard. And she fixed bouquets in these lovely pink goblets. And she had two to a table. Well, Elsa put on pastel striped tablecloth. And I had made woven... I had woven with their nylon and cotton oh, their parts of stockings. And then I dyed them different pastel colors and made potholes woven, you know, on the loom. And so we had those on the table and Flora put them so they were diagonal. And on that Mariel and Flora had fixed nut cups. They were rather large like that and they had tied them with some pretty ribbon and had a little sprig of artificial flower and a little butterfly. And that... we put candies and nuts and had that on that on the pothole. Oh, the table was pretty.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Sounds like it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And it was just as pretty as it could be. Kay Kimball sat opposite me. We were talking and Kay said, you know... She said, we have experienced three remarkable things in our lifetime. She says, you know, we're very fortunate to have been able to. And she said, the first was man walking on the moon. She said, the second was the total eclipse. And the third was the eruption of Mount St. Helens. Of course, that was the first, you know, in March. And I said, yes, Kay, you are. You're so right. That it... You know, ordinarily, if something outstanding like man walking on the moon would be only one thing that would happen. And I said, not only that, Kay, but you probably don't did experience, but I said I did. Lindbergh flying across the Atlantic in that little airplane which I saw in Washington, D.C. And it was just like a toy. And I said, we're in the atomic age. I said, when I was in college, only 12 people understood Einstein's theory of relativity. And I said, now look, we have atomic energy. I said, at the time I was taking physics, the atom hadn't been split yet. The energy of it had not been put to use. And I said, we have. I said, look at all the wonderful things that we have experienced. And that was the day before the May 18th eruption. At the picnic, I told Kay, I said, you know, we should have had the luncheon a week later. Then we could have added the real eruption to our list. But there's something new all the time. It's something that when you think of people committing suicide, how could anybody do that? Sure, you can become depressed. There are problems. We have world problems. There's starvation. But it's for us to do something about it, to try to help, to alleviate it. Perhaps some of it we can't because due to ignorance. But then maybe we could even do something about that. We must always, always strive. We must never give up. And that's the sort of thing I miss, being involved, you see, with young people to help them to realize that life is wonderful. And I think of poor Kenny Feller. Yeah. How troubled that boy must have been. And his life was just starting.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He hadn't experienced so many things, you know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, was he a boy that, was he mentally sick, or was it that he didn't have anybody to communicate with, or what was the problem?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I really don't know, Sylvia. That really came as a shock to me. I didn't have Kenny in a class that year.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So I'd only see him about every six weeks or so at class meetings because I was their class advisor. And he just, you know, he seemed fine there at the beginning of the year, but then, you know, I noticed that he was getting really quiet and stuff, you know, and I'd go up to him and I'd say, Ken, what's the matter, you know? Is there something troubling or anything I can do? And, well, no, no, no, and he just would kind of leave. And I don't know. I guess I personally feel a little guilty over what happened. But, you know, I tried to communicate with him, and he was just a very quiet and to himself boy. It hit me pretty hard.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, well, of course, you can't blame yourself for it. Oh, yeah. Because that was an act that he did on his own. And actually, you come right down to it, he was responsible for it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But, you know, we've never,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: we haven't ever in our community here had, well, I don't remember of anything to equal it. Of course, I know that in the family there, Ron was having drinking problems, but he was taking care of that. And, of course, I've always maintained alcohol is one of the worst drugs there are. And yet, you can't eliminate, because it's in the Bible, they had the alcohol, they had the wine, and wine was an important part of the biblical times, and so on.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Just like overeating, too. Food can be.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm right there.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, dear. If I ever learn to shut that table, I like to cook, and I like what I cook.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I hear you.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How's the food at school?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, fine. I think we're probably about done with this.
